title: How to Write a Welding Estimate (with Example Line Items)
description: Step-by-step guide to writing welding estimates — process rates for stick, MIG, TIG and flux-core, steel and consumables markup, hour-estimating methods, deposit and payment terms, with example line items.
h1: How to Write a Welding Estimate
intro: A welding estimate has to price four different things at once — arc time by process, steel and consumables at markup, prep hours that nobody sees, and the deposit that protects you on fabrication work. This guide walks through every field a complete welding estimate needs, with real line-item examples for repair work, shop fabrication, and mobile on-site jobs.

sections.h2: What every welding estimate must include

blocks.text: Beyond the standard fields (business name, client, date, totals), a welding estimate should carry trade-specific details that prevent disputes and protect both warranty and pricing:

items: Weld process per task — SMAW (stick), FCAW (flux-core), GMAW (MIG), or GTAW (TIG) — because hourly rates differ by process and skill required
Material spec and grade — e.g. A36 mild steel, 304/316 stainless, 6061-T6 aluminum — priced at cost plus 20–30% markup
Consumables and shielding gas as a separate line — electrode (E7018, ER70S-6), wire, argon/CO₂ mixes — so the client sees the pass-through
Prep and finishing hours — cutting, beveling, fit-up, grinding, and paint or coating — often 30–50% of total labor
Mobilization fee for field work — truck, rig, and travel time, with a minimum call-out
Valid-until date (30 days is standard — steel prices move), deposit terms, and workmanship warranty period on welded joints

blocks.text: Listing the process per line matters more than most welders expect: a client who sees "TIG on 304 stainless" as its own line understands why that task costs twice what a stick weld on mild steel does. It also documents exactly what work the estimate covers if the scope is questioned later.

sections.h2: Common welding line items (with sample rates)

blocks.text: Rates vary by region, certification, and whether the work is shop or field. These are national midpoints from 2024–2025 contractor pricing surveys — adjust to your overhead and local market.

Certified welders command the top of each range — AWS D1.1 (structural), ASME Section IX (pressure vessel), and API 1104 (pipe) certifications justify 15–30% premiums because the work is inspectable and code-bound. If you hold a code certification, say so on the estimate itself; it is the cheapest price-justification you will ever write.
Most underpriced welding jobs come from guessing arc time instead of calculating it. Two methods cover most shop and field work:

items: Pound-of-deposit method — figure the weld deposit weight, then divide by your deposition rate. A 1/4" fillet weld deposits roughly 0.75 lb of steel per foot; a field welder running stick deposits 3–5 lb/hr, a shop MIG setup 8–10 lb/hr. A 40-foot 1/4" fillet is ~30 lb ≈ 3–10 arc hours depending on process and position.

Footage method — measure joint length from the drawing and apply your measured feet-per-hour for the same joint type and position. Horizontal flat 1/4" fillets run far faster than overhead or vertical-up; price position work at 60–70% of flat speed.
Prep and fit-up — add 30–50% of arc time for cutting, beveling, tacking, and clamping. Repair work on rusty or painted steel runs higher — grinding to clean metal is billable time.
Contingency — for anything you cannot fully see (repairs, unknown base metal), add 15–25% and label the estimate as subject to inspection.

blocks.text: Track actual hours against estimated hours on every job for a few months. Most shops find their real deposition rates are 20–30% below the handbook numbers once positioning, electrode changes, and cleanup are counted — that gap is exactly the margin you are currently giving away.

Shop work prices at a lower hourly rate ($50–$85) because the welder controls position, prep equipment, and throughput — but quote it as a firm price where possible. Drawings let you calculate footage exactly, so a shop estimate can usually be converted to a fixed quote the client can sign.

Field work carries a higher rate ($75–$125) plus mobilization: the truck, engine drive, and travel are real costs. Most mobile welders set a minimum call-out of $150–$300 and bill travel beyond a set radius at an hourly rate. State the minimum clearly on the estimate — it filters non-serious calls before you burn a trip.

sections.h2: Estimate vs. quote vs. bid — which to send

blocks.text: An estimate is a good-faith price range that can move with actual hours and materials — right for repair work where you cannot see the full damage until you grind into it. A quote is a fixed price held for a stated period (usually 30 days) — right for shop fabrication off a drawing. A bid is a formal proposal, usually against other bidders, on larger or contract work — right for structural and code-inspected projects.

In practice: send an estimate with a firm materials figure and a labor range for repairs; convert to a quote the moment the scope is defined; use a bid package with WPS (welding procedure specification) references when the job is code-inspected. The same template works for all three — change the title and how firm you make the numbers.

sections.h2: Deposits and payment terms for fabrication work

blocks.text: Welding carries real up-front cost — steel and consumables are bought before the first arc strikes. Standard terms that protect the shop:

items: 50% deposit at signing for fabrication and material purchases — enough to cover steel, gas, and consumables in full
Net 10–30 on the balance, with the warranty period starting at final payment
Progress billing on multi-week jobs — bill at milestones (materials delivered, fit-up complete, final pass) instead of one lump sum
Retainage of 5–10% on contract work, released after inspection sign-off — quote it into the price, not after
Workmanship warranty of 90 days on welded joints is standard; longer warranties only where you control the coating and environment

blocks.text: Put the deposit line on the estimate itself, shown as a separate amount — "50% deposit due at signing: $612.50" converts far better than a percentage buried in the terms. Clients decide on the deposit while they are deciding on the job, not after.

sections.h2: Sales tax on welding and fabrication

blocks.text: Sales tax on welding is genuinely inconsistent across states, and it turns on whether the work is classified as fabrication of tangible goods (usually taxable), a repair to real property (varies), or new construction (often exempt). Texas, for example, taxes fabricated items and repair labor on tangible personal property; many states exempt repair labor on real property but tax the materials. The practical rule: set the taxable flag per line item — materials and consumables taxable in most states, labor taxable in some — rather than applying one rate to the total, and check your state DOR before your first job in a new classification.

faq.q: How do I estimate a welding job cost?
faq.a: Break the job into weld processes (stick, MIG, TIG, flux-core), estimate hours for each from joint footage and deposition rate, then add prep time (cutting, beveling, fit-up) at 30–50% of arc time, materials at cost plus 20–30%, consumables and gas, and mobilization if on-site. Multiply hours by your shop or field rate, add a 50% deposit line for fabrication, and set a 30-day valid-until date.

faq.q: How much should I charge per hour for welding?
faq.a: Typical US ranges: stick/SMAW $50–$75/hr, flux-core $60–$85/hr, MIG $60–$90/hr, and TIG on stainless or aluminum $75–$125/hr. Shop rates run lower than field rates, which should cover travel and equipment. Certified welders (AWS D1.1, ASME IX, API 1104) command the top of each range — and can justify a 15–30% premium on code work.

faq.q: Should I send an estimate or a quote?
faq.a: Send an estimate when you cannot see the full scope — repairs, rusted or painted steel, unknown base metal. Send a fixed quote when a drawing lets you calculate joint footage exactly, typically shop fabrication. For code-inspected or contract work, submit a formal bid with WPS references. The same template covers all three — adjust the title and how firm the numbers are.

faq.q: How much deposit should I ask for on welding work?
faq.a: 50% at signing is standard for fabrication, because it covers steel, gas, and consumables bought before work starts. For pure repair labor with minimal materials, 25–30% or a minimum call-out is common. On multi-week jobs, switch to progress billing at milestones instead of one deposit.
